text:
Is supersonic travel actually coming back? Boom Supersonic's Overture project is striving to do just that and deliver a commercial supersonic airliner that makes financial sense, especially now as the company has moved beyond the XB-1 demonstration phase and into the world of real airliner production. It is no longer enough to rely on the excitement of speed alone; the focus now shifts to whether the Overture can survive the harsh economic realities that eventually grounded the Concorde.

The history of commercial supersonic travel is littered with technical marvels that failed as business models. Boom Supersonic has achieved notable milestones, such as the XB-1 reaching supersonic speeds in 2025, but going from these somewhat small achievements in the grand scheme of things to a mass-produced, 64–80 passenger airliner is an entirely different scale of challenge. This article will explore whether Boom can navigate the certification of both a clean-sheet airframe and an all-new engine simultaneously, all while proving that high-speed travel can be profitable in an era currently defined by operational efficiency and rigorous sustainability targets.

The Long Road Ahead

Boom Supersonic has proven that the aerodynamics for supersonic flight are viable with the XB-1, but expanding that into a passenger airliner remains a profound challenge. The independence of a startup allows for rapid innovation, but it also strips away the massive institutional support and decades of certification expertise that companies like Boeing or Airbus hold. Like with any startup project, the engineering hurdles are surmountable, though the economic and certification risks create a narrow path for success, making the Overture, at least for now, a moonshot rather than something that can be fully validated.

Unlike the government-subsidized development of the Concorde, which prioritized national prestige over profit, the Overture will need to satisfy private investors and airline balance sheets from day one. Boom is attempting to certify a clean-sheet airframe and a proprietary engine, the Symphony, simultaneously, a process that has historically consumed over 10 years for established giants. The reliance on non-binding orders from carriers like United Airlines, American Airlines, and Japan Airlines suggests genuine interest, but these agreements provide little protection against the inevitable delays and cost overruns inherent in clean-sheet aerospace manufacturing.

The true test lies in whether Boom can scale production to meet its ambitious timeline without the luxury of a legacy supply chain or a global maintenance network. History shows that even with superior technology, an aircraft can fail if it lacks a robust ecosystem to support it in operation. If the Overture arrives late, costs more than anticipated, or fails to integrate seamlessly into existing airport infrastructure, its speed advantage will be secondary to its economic failure, echoing the lessons of the Concorde era, where technical brilliance was overshadowed by commercial isolation.

Flying Fast Is Not Enough

The engineering challenge of breaking the sound barrier is often the primary focus when making an aircraft fly at supersonic speeds, but the true hurdle for Boom lies in integrating a high-speed, specialized aircraft into a global network built for subsonic reliability. For an airline, every one of these factors - fuel burn, parts availability, and airport compatibility - acts as a potential friction point that could turn a technical marvel into a financial liability.

Boom will need to prove that the Overture is more than just a faster airplane and is something that is a viable fleet asset like any of the other widely used commercial aircraft in service today. The company has shown a commitment to 100% sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to meet modern emissions mandates, which currently face significant supply constraints and may prove to be a challenge if supply does not improve. Also, the establishment of a global maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) network that can support a clean-sheet design is something that will take many years to achieve, especially given the robustness of what a manufacturer like Airbus or Boeing has.

Additionally, the ability to ramp up production to a target of 33 to 66 aircraft annually to achieve necessary economies of scale will not be easy in a time of production backlogs across the industry. Unlike legacy manufacturers, Boom does not have a 50-year legacy of airport ground support or spare parts logistics to lean on, making every operational decision a test of the company's ability to build an entire support ecosystem from scratch.

The cautionary tale here is the Airbus A380, which serves as a stark reminder of the risks associated with highly specialized aircraft. Much like the Overture aims to be, the A380 was an engineering masterpiece that demanded unique airport infrastructure, specialized gate configurations, and high-density passenger loads to be profitable. When market demand shifted or operational costs spiked, the A380 became a logistical burden for many carriers who found it too expensive to operate on routes that did not perfectly fit its high-capacity niche. For Boom, the danger is that the Overture could similarly find itself isolated, a premium asset that only makes financial sense on a handful of specific long-haul routes, leaving operators exposed if global travel patterns or fuel costs fluctuate unexpectedly.

Preparing For The Worst

The relationship between Boom Supersonic and major carriers like United, American, and Japan Airlines is best described as a strategic hedge. While these airlines have placed a combined 130 conditional orders and pre-orders for the Overture, these agreements are largely designed to secure a spot in line with minimal financial risk. For the airlines, the public relations benefit of appearing future-forward is significant, but there is a clear consensus among leadership that it is too early to go all in. It seems this small group of airlines is not banking their fleets on a 2029 entry-into-service date; instead, they are keeping a window open, allowing them to make a move instantly if Boom encounters the certification or manufacturing delays that history suggests are almost inevitable.

Independent analysts, such as those at Forecast International, hold a far more skeptical view than the optimistic timelines presented in Boom’s press releases. The central concern is the lack of precedent: no company, not even aerospace giants like Boeing or Airbus, has simultaneously certified a clean-sheet airframe and an all-new engine on such an aggressive schedule. The 2030 target is widely considered highly speculative, with many experts anticipating a drift into the 2030s. The technical burden of proof for the Symphony engine, coupled with the rigorous testing required for the airframe, leaves a very narrow margin for the inevitable engineering setbacks that accompany revolutionary aerospace projects.

Interestingly, Boom has demonstrated a shrewd survival instinct by diversifying its engine technology, which adds a layer of credibility that many startups lack. Taking advantage of the Symphony engine’s core technology for industrial power generation, a program dubbed Superpower, Boom is creating a secondary revenue stream that does not rely on the Overture taking flight. Where this may come in handy is that it is a vital safety net; even if the Overture faces multi-year delays or certification hurdles, the company has built a viable, standalone business in the energy sector. It suggests that while the supersonic dream is the headline, Boom’s leadership is pragmatically preparing for a reality where the supersonic revolution takes much longer, or arrives in a different form, than originally promised.

Can It Compare To What Is Already Available?

The most immediate competitor to the Overture is not another supersonic startup, but the highly refined, ultra-premium subsonic experience currently offered by major legacy carriers. The choice for travelers often boils down to a fundamental trade-off of speed versus the ability to work, sleep, and remain productive for the duration of a flight. Modern business and first-class cabins on aircraft like the Airbus A350 or Boeing 787 are essentially mobile offices and bedrooms, designed to make a 10-hour flight feel like a controlled environment where productivity is maximized. The Overture, by contrast, prioritizes the rapid crossing of the ocean, potentially sacrificing the third space comfort that has become the peak for long-haul travel.

The pros of the Overture are obvious; cutting flight times in half is a clear win for those whose time is the ultimate currency. However, the cons are equally significant when placed against the flying hotel standard of modern subsonic aviation. An Overture flight, with its narrower fuselage and 64 to 80 passenger capacity, cannot replicate the space, privacy, or amenities of a current widebody premium cabin. Travelers who prioritize the experience of a flight, the ability to enjoy a multi-course meal, change into pajamas, and get seven hours of uninterrupted sleep may find the Overture’s cramped, high-speed environment to be an inconvenience rather than an upgrade. It is a well-thought-through transit solution, whereas the current business class is a far better lifestyle solution.

The view of the Overture being a niche asset is reinforced when you compare it to the current trend of super-first-class suites, which are seeing a resurgence among top-tier global airlines. While Boom pushes for speed, the market is moving toward more luxurious, private, and spacious cabin configurations. For the vast majority of premium passengers, the pain of a longer flight is already solved by comfort, not just velocity. If the Overture can only compete on time and not on the quality of the journey, it will likely struggle to win over the high-value passengers who have become accustomed to the flying hotel level of service.

Managing The Current Reality Of Aircraft Production

The path to commercial viability is not just paved with engineering hurdles, but with a complex web of evolving regulatory and environmental constraints. Boom Supersonic has achieved critical milestones, but the Overture will need to contend with an aerospace certification environment that is more rigorous than anything seen during the Concorde era. A major risk remains the integration of the clean-sheet Symphony engine because, unlike established OEMs that can iterate on proven engine cores, Boom must certify both the engine and airframe at the same time. It naturally creates a compounding risk profile, where a setback in propulsion development can stall the entire airframe program, leaving the company vulnerable to funding gaps and timeline slips that are common in startup ventures.

Environmental and noise compliance is another significant drawback that could limit the aircraft’s operational footprint. The FAA recently took steps in July 2026 to propose a framework for overland supersonic flight based on noise levels rather than a blanket speed ban. These rules are, however, performance-based and require operators to prove that sonic booms reaching the surface remain below strict overpressure limits. Even if Boom achieves this, individual airports retain proprietary authority to restrict operations based on local noise concerns. The Overture’s ability to use existing subsonic infrastructure is a key design goal, but its actual noise footprint, specifically during takeoff and landing, will be subject to the same increasingly stringent ICAO noise standards that govern today’s subsonic fleets.

If the Overture manages to carve out a foothold, it could easily bring with it a fundamental bifurcation in the premium market: one segment for the time-poor traveler who views transit speed as the ultimate luxury, and another for the experience-driven flyer who views the subsonic cabin as a sanctuary for rest. The success of the Overture may therefore rest not on replacing subsonic travel, but on successfully coexisting with it by positioning itself as an ultra-niche, time-saving tool rather than a comprehensive replacement for the current, comfort-first flying experience.

What Lies In Front For The Overture

The reality of Boom’s Overture is that it is still a risky engineering endeavor that has yet to prove itself as a sustainable financial model. The company has achieved critical technical milestones, most notably with the XB-1 demonstrator, but the transition from prototype to a mass-produced, 64 to 80 passenger airliner is an entirely different operational mountain to climb. Supersonic travel is technically possible, but it is not yet economically inevitable, and whether this project marks the return of the Concorde era or simply a footnote in aviation history will depend on the firm's ability to navigate the complex certification of the Symphony engine and the sheer volatility of commercial aviation economics.

Looking forward, the most critical indicator of success is not the speed of the aircraft, but the maturity of the engine development program. Certification of an all-new engine is a gargantuan task that has historically sidelined or exhausted even the largest aerospace manufacturers. For investors and prospective airline operators, the focus must remain on the Symphony engine’s testing progress rather than the sleek, promotional renders of the Overture itself. If Boom can prove that its powerplants are reliable, maintainable, and efficient enough to operate at a lower cost-per-seat-mile than the Concorde, then the supersonic dream has a chance of becoming a reality.

In the coming years, expect to see a measured, cautious approach from the major airlines that have placed conditional orders. As the planned 2029 to 2030 entry-into-service date approaches, these carriers will be looking for concrete proof of certification timelines and firm operational cost data. The Overture is currently a visionary proposition, and rightly so; it is an ambitious attempt to disrupt a mature industry that values predictability above all else. If it succeeds, it will be because Boom transformed supersonic travel from a prestige project into a repeatable, scalable business, a feat that has never been accomplished in the history of commercial flight.

title: Jet Fuel Shock Tests Wizz Air and Low Cost Travel
description:
Fuel Prices Rise Into the Spotlight Again Jet fuel has long been one of the largest components of an airline’s operating expenses, and recent volatility has thrust it back to the center of the aviation story.
Wizz Air Feels the Heat From Jet Fuel and Capacity Constraints Among Europe’s big low cost players, Wizz Air has recently been singled out by analysts as especially vulnerable to energy market swings.
When jet fuel prices spiked again, that approach exposed Wizz Air more directly to the spot market than airlines that had locked in a larger share of their needs in advance.
The airline is also grappling with broader operational headwinds that make passing on fuel costs more complex.
For low cost carriers like Wizz Air and Ryanair, the core value proposition is unlikely to disappear, but it may shift.
text:
Surging jet fuel costs and mounting concerns over physical supply are colliding with Europe’s low cost airline boom, putting fresh pressure on carriers such as Wizz Air, Ryanair and their global peers and prompting questions over whether the era of ultra cheap air travel can endure.

Fuel Prices Rise Into the Spotlight Again

Jet fuel has long been one of the largest components of an airline’s operating expenses, and recent volatility has thrust it back to the center of the aviation story. Industry data from global trade bodies and energy analysts indicates that jet fuel prices, which had eased from their post‑pandemic peaks, climbed sharply again in late 2025 and early 2026 as wider oil markets tightened and supply chains were disrupted by geopolitical tensions. In parallel, new reports flag the risk of localized jet fuel shortages in parts of Europe during the coming summer peak, a significant concern for carriers that already run on thin margins.

Published analysis of airline financials shows that even in relatively benign years fuel typically accounts for between one third and almost half of operating costs at leading low cost carriers. When prices jump or physical supply becomes constrained, those cost shocks can no longer be absorbed quietly in the background. They either erode profitability, force airlines to trim capacity, or translate into higher ticket prices for travelers. With global passenger demand returning solidly above pre‑pandemic levels, the timing of this renewed fuel squeeze is particularly sensitive.

Industry outlooks for 2026 still anticipate that airlines as a whole will remain profitable, but they also stress that margins are likely to stay slim and highly exposed to fuel dynamics. As a result, how airlines manage their exposure to jet fuel has become a defining competitive issue for the next phase of the recovery, especially for budget operators that compete primarily on price.

Wizz Air Feels the Heat From Jet Fuel and Capacity Constraints

Among Europe’s big low cost players, Wizz Air has recently been singled out by analysts as especially vulnerable to energy market swings. Publicly available commentary on the carrier’s strategy indicates that it has continued to expand rapidly into Central and Eastern Europe and the Middle East, often with thinner hedging cover than its main rivals. When jet fuel prices spiked again, that approach exposed Wizz Air more directly to the spot market than airlines that had locked in a larger share of their needs in advance.

Reports on the current jet fuel crunch suggest that Wizz Air has now covered a substantial portion of its 2026 fuel requirements through hedging contracts, but at prices that are well above the pre‑crisis norm. While that protects the airline against further spikes, it also crystallizes higher costs for the near term. In an ultra low cost model where base fares are aggressively discounted and ancillary charges carry much of the profit, there is limited room to absorb such increases without some combination of fare rises, new fees or cost cutting in other parts of the business.

The airline is also grappling with broader operational headwinds that make passing on fuel costs more complex. Engine reliability problems on parts of the Airbus A320neo family and ongoing aircraft delivery delays have constrained capacity just as demand for sun destinations and city breaks is booming. For Wizz Air, that has meant juggling schedule resilience, crew availability and network growth while fuel costs climb, a balancing act that investors are watching closely.

For travelers, the near term impact is likely to be felt most acutely on thinner routes from secondary cities, where Wizz Air faces less direct competition. Those are the markets where the carrier has more pricing power and where any decision to trim unprofitable flying because of fuel costs can quickly translate into reduced choice and higher average fares.

Ryanair and Other Low Cost Giants Lean on Hedging

Ryanair, Europe’s largest airline by passenger numbers, offers a contrasting case study in how fuel strategy can buffer a carrier from market shocks. The group’s recent financial results show robust profits and emphasize a “conservative” jet fuel hedging approach, with around 80 percent of its needs reportedly locked in at about 67 dollars a barrel through early 2027. That level of protection has allowed Ryanair to present itself publicly as relatively insulated from the latest price surge.

By securing fuel at significantly below current spot levels, Ryanair has widened its cost advantage over competitors that are more exposed to the market. Company filings and investor presentations stress that higher fuel prices are likely to hit unhedged rivals harder, potentially forcing them to cut capacity or raise fares. In contrast, Ryanair has signaled that it plans to keep stimulating demand with competitive prices while gradually nudging average fares higher where the market will bear it.

Other low cost carriers, including easyJet in Europe and Southwest in the United States, have similarly highlighted hedging as a key defense, although their coverage levels and contract prices differ. Legacy airlines often hedge less aggressively or over shorter horizons, leaving them more exposed to short term spikes but giving more flexibility if prices fall. The divergence in strategies means that the same fuel shock can have very different implications across the industry.

For passengers, this patchwork of hedging positions helps explain why airfares are rising faster on some routes and with some airlines than others. Well hedged carriers can afford to be “load active” by keeping planes full with competitive fares and using ancillary revenues to support margins, at least while their hedges last. Those with less protection may move sooner to increase ticket prices, add surcharges or trim their schedules.

Global Airlines Confront a New Cost Landscape

The pressure is not confined to Europe. Major airlines in North America, Asia and the Pacific have also issued earnings guidance reflecting sharply higher fuel bills. Publicly available financial updates from United States carriers show that several now expect billions of dollars in additional fuel expenses for 2026 compared with earlier forecasts, citing both crude price increases and widening refining margins for jet fuel.

In the Asia Pacific region, carriers exposed to long haul routes are particularly sensitive to sustained high fuel prices, given the greater fuel burn over intercontinental distances. Airlines serving island nations and remote destinations, where alternative transport options are limited, face the difficult choice of either passing on more of these costs or cutting back on marginal routes that are important for tourism.

At the same time, airlines worldwide are under rising pressure to invest in cleaner technology and sustainable aviation fuel. Those investments are necessary for long term climate goals but they also add to near term cost burdens. Sustainable aviation fuels remain several times more expensive than conventional jet fuel, and policy frameworks in Europe and other regions are gradually increasing minimum blending requirements, effectively raising the floor under airlines’ fuel bills over time.

Industry economic assessments suggest that, even with strong demand, global airline margins in 2026 will remain in low single digits once fuel, labor, maintenance and financing costs are fully accounted for. In such an environment, there is little cushion to absorb further shocks without some effect on ticket prices, particularly for price sensitive leisure and visiting‑friends‑and‑relatives markets that rely heavily on low fares.

Is the Era of Ultra Cheap Travel Ending?

The key question for travelers is whether soaring fuel costs mark the end of the rock bottom fares that defined the rise of low cost airlines over the past two decades. Evidence from fare trackers and consumer price indices suggests that, after adjusting for inflation, average airfares remained relatively subdued for much of the past decade, even as fuel costs fluctuated. Many airlines chose to protect market share and stimulate demand by absorbing part of those cost swings in their margins.

The latest fuel shock, coupled with aircraft supply constraints and climate regulations, points toward a different trajectory. Analysts now widely expect that the very lowest promotional fares, particularly on peak summer dates and popular leisure routes, will become less frequent. Instead, airlines are likely to focus on carefully managing capacity, keeping load factors high and using sophisticated revenue management to push up average yields while still advertising headline bargains in limited quantities.

For low cost carriers like Wizz Air and Ryanair, the core value proposition is unlikely to disappear, but it may shift. Travelers may continue to see attractive base fares between major cities, yet pay more in total once luggage, seat selection and other extras are included. On thinner regional routes where competition is limited and fuel represents a higher share of total costs, some services may be reduced or consolidated, making cheap spontaneous trips harder to find.

Looking ahead to the next few seasons, the balance between fuel markets, airline hedging strategies and regulatory pressures will shape how far and how fast ticket prices rise. For now, cheap travel is not vanishing, but it is becoming more conditional, more seasonal and more unevenly distributed. Passengers willing to be flexible on dates, destinations and departure airports may still find deals, while those bound to peak times and specific routes are likely to face steadily firmer price tags.

title: Egypt promotes investment, trade opportunities during BRICS Trade Ministers meeting
description:
Investment Minister Mohamed Farid held meetings with his counterparts on the sidelines of the 16th BRICS Trade Ministers meeting.
During the meetings, Farid emphasized that Egypt was keen to revive its business councils with several BRICS members.
Egypt, India eye deeper trade, investment ties Minister of Investment Mohamed Farid met with India’s Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal to discuss bilateral trade, joint investments, and technology transfer.
Farid also discussed strengthening cooperation between Egypt and India in pharmaceutical manufacturing, including oncology drugs and immunosuppressants.
As of 2025, Egypt and India’s trade volume recorded around $4.18 billion.
text:
Investment Minister Mohamed Farid held meetings with his counterparts on the sidelines of the 16th BRICS Trade Ministers meeting.

BRICS is an intergovernmental organization that aims to increase economic cooperation between emerging markets in the Global South. It includes Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, and Indonesia.

Egypt has been a BRICS member state since 2024.

During the meetings, Farid emphasized that Egypt was keen to revive its business councils with several BRICS members.

Egypt, India eye deeper trade, investment ties

Minister of Investment Mohamed Farid met with India’s Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal to discuss bilateral trade, joint investments, and technology transfer.

Farid also discussed strengthening cooperation between Egypt and India in pharmaceutical manufacturing, including oncology drugs and immunosuppressants. He also discussed potential cooperation between the two nations in manufacturing fertilizers.

Egypt aims to attract Indian investment in production projects. It hopes to increase trade with India to $12 billion within the next five years. As of 2025, Egypt and India’s trade volume recorded around $4.18 billion.

The Egyptian government aims to increase annual exports to $115.8 billion by 2030 and raise non-oil exports by 15–20 percent annually through 2030.

During the first eleven months of FY2025/2026, which ended at the end of June 2026, Egypt's trade deficit narrowed by 7.6 percent to almost EGP 1 trillion.

Moreover, Farid discussed convening the seventh session of the Egyptian-Indian Joint Trade Committee in 2026. He revealed that both sides have discussed plans to establish an Indian Industrial Zone within the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZone).

Egypt’s investment minister also met with members of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce (FICCI), which includes firms such as TCI Sanmar Chemicals, clean energy developer Ocior Energy, optical fiber integrator Sterlite, conglomerate ITC Limited, and petroleum refining and marketing firm Reliance Industries.

Farid urged Indian companies to take advantage of Egypt’s location and free trade agreements to establish large-scale investment projects in manufacturing chemicals, energy and electricity grids, food processing, strategic grain storage, consumer goods, and infrastructure.

UAE cooperation targets digital transformation

Egypt’s investment minister discussed plans to develop digital transformation and automation of government services with his Emirati counterpart, Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi.

Egypt plans to draw on the UAE’s expertise in developing digital platforms to streamline service delivery and procedures for investors.

The two sides also discussed increasing investments, trade partnerships, and joint initiatives.

The UAE has recently increased investments in the Egyptian market, especially in real estate projects such as Ras El-Hekma.

Trade between the two countries reached around $9.68 billion in 2025. Egyptian exports to the UAE rose to around $6.88 billion in 2025, up from $1.22 billion in 2021, marking a 475 percent increase. Egyptian imports from the UAE rose to $2.69 billion in 2025, up from $2.46 billion in 2021.

A delegation from the UAE International Investors Council (UAEIIC) is expected to visit Egypt to explore available and new investment instruments and discuss establishing new partnerships across priority sectors, such as advanced infrastructure and industrial and logistics zones.

Egypt seeks greater access to Chinese market

On the sidelines of the BRICS meeting, Farid met with China’s Vice Minister of Commerce Li Chenggang, with whom he discussed increasing Egyptian exports’ access to the Chinese market and Chinese investments in productive sectors in Egypt.

The two sides also discussed the participation of Egyptian companies in the China International Fair for Investment and Trade (CIFIT) and the China International Import Expo (CIIE). They also discussed the best ways Egyptian companies can benefit from China's full exemption of Egyptian exports from tariffs.

China is one of Egypt’s largest trading partners, with bilateral trade reaching $19.52 billion in 2025.

Egypt, Russia discuss grain cooperation

Farid also held a meeting with Russian Deputy Minister of Economic Development Vladimir Ilichev to discuss expanding work in the grain sector.

Cairo is working to strengthen its strategic grain reserves, diversify wheat sources, and expand local procurement. Russia has remained Egypt’s leading wheat supplier in recent years, accounting for a significant share of purchases made through both state tenders and private contracts.

Egyptian exports to Russia increased from $485 million in 2021 to approximately $811 million by 2025, representing an increase of around 66 percent, while the trade volume between the two nations reached $5.7 billion in 2025.

Egypt, Brazil explore biofuel, energy partnerships

Similarly, Egypt's investment minister held talks with Brazilian Minister of Industrial Development, Trade, and Services Márcio Fernando Elias Rosa, with whom he discussed cooperation in tourism, trade, and energy refining.

The two sides plan to increase cooperation in manufacturing sustainable aviation fuel to establish Egypt as a regional hub for supplying ships with low-carbon fuels, specifically providing biofuels to vessels transiting the Suez Canal.

Egypt plans to rely on Brazil to provide technical presentations on the product and its advantages.

title: Denmark Travel Surges as SAS Leads Europe in Reliability
description:

This rebound has helped offset a slight moderation in purely domestic travel and has reinforced Denmark’s role as a gateway to Scandinavia.

text:
Denmark is experiencing a surge in visitor numbers as Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) emerges among Europe’s most reliable major carriers, creating smoother journeys into Copenhagen and across Scandinavia just as demand for Nordic travel accelerates.

Record Tourism Strengthens Denmark’s Position in Europe

Recent tourism data indicate that Denmark has consolidated its status as one of Northern Europe’s strongest performers, with overnight stays surpassing pre‑pandemic levels and setting new records in both 2023 and 2024. Statistics from national authorities and VisitDenmark show that total tourist overnights have climbed into the mid‑60 million range annually, reflecting steady year‑on‑year growth and renewed appetite for Nordic city breaks and coastal stays.

International demand is a key driver. Reports from Denmark’s official tourism bodies show that foreign visitors now account for more than half of total commercial overnight stays, with particular strength from neighboring Germany, the Netherlands and the Nordic region. This rebound has helped offset a slight moderation in purely domestic travel and has reinforced Denmark’s role as a gateway to Scandinavia.

Policymakers and industry groups highlight that the recovery has occurred alongside a push for more balanced, year‑round tourism rather than purely summer‑focused peaks. Published strategies from VisitDenmark stress spreading demand across the calendar and across the country, from Copenhagen and Aarhus to secondary coastal and nature destinations, to support jobs, local businesses and more sustainable visitor flows.

OECD tourism assessments echo these trends, noting that Denmark has moved well beyond its 2019 benchmarks and that overall tourism expenditure has risen into the equivalent of hundreds of billions of Danish kroner annually. This combination of higher volumes and stronger spending is now feeding through to airlines, airports and wider transport networks that serve the country.

SAS Climbs to the Top Tier for On‑Time Performance

As visitor numbers grow, Scandinavian Airlines has emerged as one of Europe’s most punctual major carriers, an important factor for travelers connecting through or flying directly to Denmark. Aviation analytics firm Cirium’s On‑Time Performance Review for 2024 ranked SAS in the top three among European airlines by on‑time arrivals, with an on‑time rate reported at just over 81 percent and nearly all flights tracked and completed.

Separate information published by SAS and sector media reports indicate that the airline’s punctuality held up across much of 2024, with SAS consistently appearing near the top of monthly rankings for larger European carriers. Industry coverage links that performance to the carrier’s ongoing turnaround efforts, including fleet renewal, tighter schedule planning and operational simplification following restructuring.

This reliability is critical for Denmark because SAS operates its main hub at Copenhagen Airport, handling a significant share of feeder traffic from across Scandinavia and Northern Europe. High punctuality improves onward connections to domestic Danish airports and to long‑haul destinations in North America and Asia, reducing missed connections and knock‑on delays at a time when many global hubs are still working through congestion.

Aviation analysts note that SAS’s performance stands out in a European market that has faced repeated strains from air traffic control constraints, weather disruptions and capacity bottlenecks. For travelers choosing between carriers on competitive routes into Scandinavia, the consistency of on‑time arrivals is becoming a more visible differentiator, especially for business passengers and cruise travelers with tight itineraries.

Copenhagen Airport Handles Near‑Record Traffic with Fewer Flights

Copenhagen Airport, the primary international gateway to Denmark, has paired the tourism surge with notable operational gains of its own. The airport’s latest traffic reports show it handled close to 30 million passengers in 2024, approaching its pre‑pandemic peak, even though the number of arriving and departing aircraft remained below 2019 levels.

Publicly available figures from the airport indicate that this growth is being driven mainly by European routes, which now account for more than four out of five passengers. Airlines have upgauged aircraft on many key routes, replacing smaller models with higher‑capacity narrow‑body jets, allowing more travelers to pass through the airport without a proportional increase in takeoffs and landings.

During peak summer periods, Copenhagen has set new single‑day passenger records while keeping aircraft movements in check, a combination that airport management describes in its annual report as evidence of both strong demand and more efficient use of capacity. Transfer traffic has also rebounded, with more travelers using the hub as a stepping stone between Northern Europe and destinations across the continent and beyond.

For visitors, the operational efficiencies translate into shorter taxi times and fewer schedule disruptions, especially when paired with airlines that prioritize on‑time performance. Analysts point out that Copenhagen’s compact layout, integrated rail links and coordinated scheduling with SAS and other carriers give it an advantage over larger, more fragmented hubs.

Scandinavian Journeys Become Smoother and Better Connected

The combination of SAS’s reliability and Copenhagen’s growing hub role is reshaping how travelers move across Scandinavia. With a dense network of routes from Copenhagen to major cities in Norway, Sweden and domestic Danish destinations such as Aalborg, Billund and Bornholm, visitors arriving in Denmark increasingly use the country as a springboard for multi‑stop Nordic trips.

Published route maps and schedule data show that SAS and partner airlines offer frequent services to key Scandinavian cities, with many flights timed to facilitate short connections at Copenhagen. Higher on‑time performance reduces the risk of missed flights on these tight transfers, making it more feasible for travelers to combine, for example, a weekend in Copenhagen with hiking in Norway or cultural visits in Stockholm on a single itinerary.

Regional tourism organizations have responded by marketing cross‑border experiences that leverage this connectivity, highlighting rail links, overnight ferries and domestic flights that start or end in Denmark. Industry analyses suggest that such integrated journeys appeal in particular to long‑haul visitors from North America and Asia, who seek to see multiple Nordic capitals within one trip.

At the same time, Denmark is positioning itself as a convenient starting point for low‑impact travel within the region. Initiatives promoting rail and bus connections from Copenhagen, combined with airlines’ efforts to improve fuel efficiency and explore sustainable aviation fuel, are intended to align the tourism boom with the country’s climate ambitions.

Outlook: Strong Demand and Reliability Shape Denmark’s Next Season

Looking ahead to late 2026 and the 2027 travel seasons, industry forecasts point to continued strength in arrivals to Denmark, although at a more moderate growth rate than the immediate post‑pandemic rebound. VisitDenmark and national statistical offices expect overnight stays to remain at or above recent record levels as repeat visitors and new markets underpin demand.

For airlines and airports, the main question is whether they can maintain or improve punctuality while adding capacity. Analysts watching SAS’s ongoing transformation note that sustaining on‑time performance in a busier environment will require continued investment in fleet modernization, staffing and digital tools for real‑time operations management.

Airport planners in Copenhagen, meanwhile, are working from traffic scenarios that anticipate further growth in European and intercontinental routes, supported by the airport’s role as a primary hub for SAS and other carriers. Infrastructure upgrades, terminal refurbishments and airfield optimizations outlined in recent annual reports are aimed at keeping the passenger experience stable even on record‑setting travel days.

For travelers, the combination of robust tourism demand, a well‑connected hub and a flagship carrier recognized near the top of European punctuality rankings suggests that journeys to and through Denmark are set to become even smoother. As the country balances visitor growth with sustainability goals, reliable air links provided by SAS and its partners are likely to remain a cornerstone of Denmark’s appeal on the global travel map.

What's the deal? Twelve, the California-based startup turning carbon dioxide into low-carbon fuels, has raised a late-stage venture round from a group of mostly Japanese investors. Development Bank of Japan joined alongside Mitsui & Co., Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, Toppan Global Venture Partners, and Advantage Partners.

Why now? Led by chief executive officer Nicholas Flanders, Twelve uses CO2 electrolysis and its OpusTM technology to transform CO2, water, and renewable energy into hydrocarbons. Its flagship product, E-Jet SAF, is a drop-in sustainable aviation fuel that works in existing aircraft with up to 90% lower lifecycle emissions than fossil-based fuel.

What it means? Twelve is building its first commercial demonstration-scale plant in Moses Lake, Washington, with operations planned to start in 2025. It has already signed offtake agreements with Alaska Airlines and IAG, and the fresh capital supports that scale-up.

What could go wrong? CO2 electrolysis is a hard technology to commercialise. While Twelve says the low-temperature process offers operational stability and adaptability to renewable energy, it remains unproven at industrial scale.

text:
The arithmetic is unforgiving. With 418 aircraft handed over through the end of July, Airbus must now deliver 452 more jets in the final five months of the year to hit its target of roughly 870 deliveries — an average of more than 90 per month. That pace would outstrip anything the manufacturer has achieved in the August-to-November window since 2023, and even last year's strong fourth-quarter sprint fell 32 aircraft short of the mark.

The July tally of 67 deliveries to 39 customers came in three units below Jefferies' internal estimate, though the brokerage maintained its "Hold" rating and €200 price target on Friday, arguing the annual goal remains within reach given an expected 8 percent acceleration in second-half output. The market appears untroubled by the math: shares closed at €214.05, up 5.42 percent over seven trading sessions and just 3.25 percent below the 52-week high of €221.25 set on January 13.

Orders Tell a Different Story

While the delivery pipeline strains, the order book is bulging. July brought 204 gross orders, including Riyadh Air's confirmation of six additional A350-1000s, a 100-aircraft commitment from leasing firm SMBC, China Eastern's order for 25 A330-900s, and six A321neos from an undisclosed customer. That pushed the first-half gross total to 886 orders, nearly double the 494 recorded a year earlier, with net orders after cancellations reaching 821 versus 402. The backlog now stands at 9,222 commercial aircraft.

The demand picture was reinforced at the Farnborough International Airshow last month, where Airbus signed a hydrogen-engine development pact with MTU Aero Engines, formed a sustainable aviation fuel joint venture with Air Canada, and launched a three-year flight test campaign using an A321neo demonstrator to trial high-aspect-ratio wings for its "Wing of Tomorrow" program — designs that would require folding wingtips to operate at existing airports.

Half-Year Results Lay the Foundation

The financials released on July 29 provide the backdrop for investor confidence. Revenue climbed 12 percent to €33.2 billion, adjusted EBIT jumped 24 percent to €2.73 billion, and net profit rose to €2.24 billion, or €2.84 per share, from €1.53 billion a year earlier. The defense and space division contributed its own momentum, with order intake more than doubling to €9.3 billion and adjusted EBIT nearly doubling to €487 million.

The cash flow picture, however, reveals the cost of accelerated production: free cash flow before customer financing came in at minus €1.17 billion, with the overall figure at minus €1.04 billion. Management nonetheless reaffirmed its full-year guidance of roughly 870 deliveries, adjusted EBIT of about €7.5 billion, and free cash flow before customer financing of approximately €4.5 billion — contingent on no further disruptions to trade, air traffic, or supply chains.

A Longer Horizon and a Bigger Buyback

The company's ambitions extend well beyond 2026. At a London presentation on July 21, Airbus laid out a target of €12 billion to €13 billion in adjusted EBIT by 2029 — nearly double the projected 2025 level — driven by plans to ramp A320neo-family production to 75 aircraft per month by 2027. Vertical Research Partners' Rob Stallard characterized the new medium-term guidance as a direct response to long-standing investor complaints about insufficient planning visibility.

The following day, the board approved a €5 billion share buyback program to run over three years. Institutional interest is building in tandem: BlackRock disclosed a 5.96 percent stake in Airbus on Wednesday, representing 47,152,884 shares, a 26.6 percent increase from its previous filing.

Operational Milestones and Setbacks

Progress continues on multiple technical fronts. Ground vibration testing for the A350F freighter was completed on August 3, a key certification step ahead of first flight. Hisdesat selected Airbus as prime contractor for SpainSat NG-III, described by the company as Europe's most advanced secure communications satellite. Airbus Helicopters also delivered its first NH90 Standard 2, configured for special operations, to French procurement agency DGA.

Not everything went smoothly. Belgium's interfederal screening committee blocked the acquisition of helicopter operator NHV Group by Irish lessor GD Helicopter Finance, which is ultimately linked to Chinese interests. NHV, the launch customer for the Airbus H175, was slated to handle maintenance subcontracting for 20 H145M helicopters ordered by Belgium — a security dimension that appears to have influenced the review.

There was also a demonstration of long-haul capability: an A350-1000ULR test aircraft flew nonstop from Toulouse to Melbourne in 19 hours and 11 minutes, a milestone for Qantas' "Project Sunrise" ultra-long-haul program.

Between now and then, the monthly delivery rate remains the single most important metric for judging whether the manufacturer can close out the year as planned.

title: What's Inside Your Fuel Tank? - Deccan Chronicle
description:

Airlines are beginning to fly on sustainable aviation fuel distilled from used cooking oil and municipal waste.

DIY HHO kits promise better mileage from tap water, yet engineers find the added alternator load actually worsens fuel economy.

text:
At a petrol pump in Nagpur, a driver watches the nozzle click off and wonders what exactly he just put in his tank. The answer, increasingly, is not simple petrol at all, but a blend shaped by chemistry, agriculture, and policy, one chapter in a much larger global search for fuel beyond crude oil.

India’s own chapter arrived early: 20% ethanol blended into petrol nationwide, made largely from sugarcane, corn, and surplus grain. Officials count it as a win: a smaller oil import bill and steady new demand for farmers.

Ethanol is hygroscopic, drawing moisture from the air, which can occasionally cause phase separation in fuel tanks, and regulators point to testing across more than 150 quality parameters as their answer.

But ethanol is only one entry in a much stranger catalogue. Airlines are beginning to fly on sustainable aviation fuel distilled from used cooking oil and municipal waste. Diesel engines are running, with barely a modification, on biodiesel made from animal fats and vegetable oil. In ponds and wastewater, microalgae are being cultivated as a ‘super fuel,’ yielding far more oil per hectare than any crop, without competing for farmland.

Rice straw and sugarcane bagasse, once burned as stubble, are being reimagined as feedstock for ethanol. Researchers have even turned to temple flower waste as a biomass source, while others chase something more elemental still: hydrogen coaxed from algae and bacteria, a fuel with no carbon at all.

10 STRANGE FUELS YOU WON’T BELIEVE HUMANS HAVE TRIED!

1. Water-powered cars: Science or myth?

Stanley Meyer’s 1990s ‘water fuel cell’ claimed to run a dune buggy on water using minimal electricity; a 1996 Ohio court found it was ordinary electrolysis and convicted him of fraud. Japan’s Genepax (2008) unveiled a similarly water-powered car, but the real fuel was expensive, self-consuming metal plates releasing hydrogen. DIY HHO kits promise better mileage from tap water, yet engineers find the added alternator load actually worsens fuel economy. To date, no water-fuel claim has survived independent scientific scrutiny; each has been debunked, discredited, or quietly abandoned.

2. Moon dust to rocket fuel

Lunar dust contains locked-up oxygen, which scientists extract using heat, electricity, or chemical reactions with astronaut-generated carbon dioxide. Since liquid oxygen makes up most of a rocket’s launch weight, mining it directly from the Moon means rockets wouldn’t need to carry it from Earth. This could turn the Moon into a refueling station, making missions to Mars lighter and far cheaper.

3. Brewtroleum: The beer that powered cars

In 2015, New Zealand’s DB Export turned leftover brewing yeast into ‘Brewtroleum,’ an E10 fuel sold at 60 Gull stations nationwide. Partnering with Refining NZ, they fermented and distilled residual sugars from spent yeast slurry into bioethanol, producing over 5 million liters at standard market prices. The campaign, “Save the World by Drinking Beer,” won Cannes Lions' Grand Prix in 2016. Though commercially successful, limited yeast supply and logistics kept it a one-run showcase of circular-economy fuel.

4. Your morning coffee could fuel tomorrow’s cars

Spent coffee grounds, dense with residual oil, are being converted into biodiesel through extraction and transesterification, meeting European and American fuel standards. London’s Bio-Bean processes up to 50,000 tonnes annually, partnering with Shell to power city buses with a B20 blend. Leftover grounds become high-heat biomass pellets. Unlike palm or soy biofuels, coffee waste competes with no food crop, offering cities a hyper-local, low-carbon fuel sourced entirely from their own daily habit.

5. From rabbits to radiators

In 2009, Stockholm faced a rabbit overpopulation crisis damaging city parks. Officials culled thousands annually, routing carcasses to a Karlskoga heating plant instead of landfills. Blended with other bio-waste, they were incinerated for district heating, sparking backlash from animal rights groups, while city officials defended it as pragmatic, zero-waste infrastructure.

6. The science of “chocolate diesel”

Confectionery waste, rich in cocoa fats, was refined and blended with vegetable oil, then transesterified into biodiesel. In a famous UK demonstration, researchers powered a modified diesel car across Europe on “chocolate fuel,” proving sugary factory scraps could sustain long-distance travel, all while its exhaust carried a faint aroma of roasted cocoa.

7. From cigarette butts to fuel blends

Cigarette filters, made of slow-degrading cellulose acetate, are being converted through pyrolysis into triacetin-rich bio-oil, a valuable diesel additive, while other processes yield bioethanol and biodiesel catalysts. Despite proven lab chemistry, scaling remains hard: butts are scattered across cities, contain thousands of toxic chemicals, and require huge volumes for meaningful fuel output.

8. The mexican nopal cactus that runs buses

In Michoacán, Mexico, company Nopalimex converts prickly pear cactus into biogas through anaerobic digestion, yielding high-purity biomethane. Requiring minimal water and avoiding food-crop land, nopal outperforms corn or sugarcane in yield and sustainability. The gas fuels municipal buses and generators in Zitácuaro, while leftover digestate returns to fields as fertilizer.

9. From hair to high power: The next waste revolution

Human hair waste, though not industrially refined as fuel, is actively collected worldwide: Australia’s Sustainable Salons supplies hair for EV battery graphite, the US-based Matter of Trust turns it into oil-spill booms, and India's Tirumala temple trust auctions tons annually for keratin and bio-fertiliser. Research hubs in India’s IITs, Australia, and Lithuania are pushing pyrolysis and supercapacitor applications, though scattered sourcing keeps hair from mainstream fuel use.

10. From Instant Noodles to Engine Fuel

In Fukuoka, Japan, logistics firm Nishida Shoun pioneered converting instant noodle and ramen waste into biofuel, powering trucks on it. Because instant noodles are pre-fried in palm oil, factory rejects and oily broth offer a high lipid content ideal for biodiesel, while easily broken-down wheat starch speeds bioethanol fermentation. The process reroutes food waste that would otherwise reach landfills, without competing with edible food supply.

text:
Company Description

About SNV

SNV is a global development partner, deeply rooted in the countries where we operate. We are driven by a vision of a better world: A world where across every society all people live with dignity and have equitable opportunities to thrive sustainably.

To make this vision a reality, we need transformations in vital agri-food, energy, and water systems. SNV contributes by strengthening capacities and catalysing partnerships in these sectors. We help strengthen institutions and effective governance, reduce gender inequalities and barriers to social inclusion, and enable adaptation and mitigation to the climate and biodiversity crises.

Building on 60 years of experience, we support our partners with our technical and process expertise and methodological rigor. We do this in more than 20 countries in Africa and Asia with a team of approximately 1,600 colleagues. By being adaptable and tailoring our approaches to these different contexts, we can contribute to impact at scale, resulting in more equitable lives for all.

SNV has been working in Vietnam since 1995 and currently has over 70 national and international experts. SNV Vietnam implements projects in more than 30 provinces across the country, including the poorest and most remote areas.

About the Study

The aviation sector faces an acute decarbonisation challenge. Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is widely recognised as the most viable near-term pathway to reducing aviation emissions at scale, yet its global scale-up is constrained by the availability of reliable, cost-competitive, and sustainably sourced feedstocks. Rice residue (straw and husks left after harvest) produced in vast quantities across the Mekong Delta of Vietnam represents one of the most promising and underexplored feedstock opportunities in Southeast Asia.

SNV Vietnam is undertaking a Comprehensive Rice-to-SAF Value Chain Feasibility Study to assess the technical, economic, environmental, and operational feasibility of mobilising rice residues at scale in Vietnam for use as SAF feedstock. The study covers 3-4 Mekong Delta provinces (including An Giang, Đồng Tháp, and Long An) and addresses five core research questions:

RQ1: Current Use & Value Mapping - how rice straw and husks are currently used and the financial/agronomic incentives required to redirect them into the SAF supply chain.

RQ2: Aggregation Bottleneck Assessment - localised logistical, financial, and infrastructure constraints to large-scale residue extraction.

RQ3: Pricing & High-Integrity Benchmarks - delivered price ranges along the supply chain, benchmarked against ICAO/CORSIA standards.

RQ4: Environmental Risk Analysis - soil health, safe extraction thresholds, and GHG modelling vs. the open-burning baseline (ICAO/CORSIA aligned).

RQ5: Offtake Feasibility & Supply Modelling - Monte Carlo simulations of supply reliability, regulatory framework review, and contract precedent analysis.

The study will draw on a substantial body of existing data and evidence alongside additional primary data collection determined necessary during the study design phase. It will also convene a formal Advisory Group (international and national members) and incorporate structured government engagement. Final outputs include a comprehensive study report, executive summary, statistical analyses, data visualisations, and Advisory Group outputs, delivered by March 2027.

SNV Vietnam is now seeking a consultant to serve as the Research and Data Lead, acting as the principal technical counterpart to the Study Manager, providing methodological leadership on survey design, enumerator training, data collection quality assurance, and statistical analysis — including the Monte Carlo supply reliability modelling that anchors the study's investment-grade evidence base.

Job Description

Objectives and Scope of Work

The Research and Data Lead will serve as the principal technical counterpart to the Study Manager and the lead in-country methodological resource for the Comprehensive Rice-to-SAF Value Chain Feasibility Study. The Research and Data Lead focuses on the technical and analytical rigour of the study, ensuring survey instruments, sampling frameworks, enumerator preparation, data quality protocols, and statistical analyses all meet the standards required for a study of this ambition.

The Research and Data Lead will work closely with the Team Lead, the SNV Global MEL Advisor, the Study Manager, other Study team members, contracted survey firms, and academic partners to carry out the following activities:

Survey design and instrument development: With guidance from the Team Leader, design and iterative refinement of all quantitative and qualitative data collection instruments — including farm household surveys, aggregator/SME questionnaires, key informant interview (KII) guides, and focus group discussion (FGD) protocols. Ensure instruments are methodologically rigorous, aligned to the study's five research questions, calibrated to Vietnamese context, and structured to enable robust downstream statistical analysis (including Monte Carlo modelling).

Sampling framework design: In partnership with the Team Lead and Global MEL Advisor, design the multi-stage stratified sampling framework for the study, including power calculations, stratification logic, and province-level allocation targets across the 3-4 target Mekong Delta provinces. Document all sampling assumptions and provide the analytical basis for scaling or adjusting samples during fieldwork.

Enumerator training and technical preparation: Design and co-deliver the technical components of enumerator training — including instrument familiarisation, survey programming/scripting, use of digital data collection platforms (e.g., ODK, KoBoToolbox, SurveyCTO), interview technique, data quality checks. Work alongside the Study Manager for selecting and contracting the survey firm and managing the logistical relationship with the contracted survey firm, to ensure enumerators are technically prepared to deliver the study to specification.

Data quality assurance during fieldwork: Serve as the principal technical monitor of data quality across the fieldwork period. Design and operate real-time data quality dashboards, review incoming data for logic errors, anomalies, and enumerator drift, flag issues for resolution with the contracted survey firm, and resolve issues with the contracted survey firm in a timely manner. Conduct spot-check field visits as required to verify data collection integrity.

Statistical analysis and modelling: Lead the statistical analysis of all primary and secondary data, including descriptive analysis, cross-tabulations, price and cost curve modelling, and inferential analysis where appropriate. Design and execute the Monte Carlo simulation of supply reliability under climate, seasonal, and offtake scenarios (RQ5), calibrating input distributions against primary survey data (farm-level yields, seasonal variations, competing uses, and aggregator capacity).

Data harmonisation and visualisation: Lead data cleaning, harmonisation across sources (primary survey data, secondary datasets, GIS layers), and the production of analytical visualisations for the study report, executive summary, and Advisory Group outputs. Ensure all analytical outputs are transparent, reproducible, and clearly documented.

Technical inputs to reporting: Contribute technical inputs to the inception report, preliminary analysis memo, comprehensive study report, and executive summary — with particular responsibility for the methodological, sampling, statistical, and Monte Carlo modelling sections. Ensure that analytical claims are appropriately caveated and that confidence ranges are transparently presented.

MEL framework support: Working under the direction of the Team Lead and Global MEL Advisor, contribute to the design and quality assurance of the overall MEL framework for the study, including analysis plans, data management protocols, and quality assurance procedures.

The Research and Data Lead will provide an estimated level of effort of up to 50 working days over the 7-month assignment period, from September 2026 to 31 March 2027. The role is Vietnam-based, with work taking place primarily in the Mekong Delta provinces (An Giang, Đồng Tháp, Long An) aligned with enumerator training, fieldwork monitoring, and validation activities.

Due Diligence Instructions

Due Diligence (DD) checks apply to individual consultants engaged by SNV for the provision of consultancy services. Conducting these checks supports SNV in managing donor funds responsibly, ethically, and in full compliance with relevant regulations. To apply, download the Microsoft Word Due Diligence and Vetting Form, click https://c.smartrecruiters.com/sr-company-attachments-prod-aws-dc5/58919688e4b0672cc03331a9/aad96d4c-3d4c-478e-8cc0-03bc9ed8e135?r=s3-eu-central-1

Qualifications

Eligibility and Qualifications

The assignment is open to individual Vietnamese national consultants who meet the following criteria:

Vietnamese national with permanent residence in Vietnam (required).

Advanced postgraduate degree (Master's required; PhD desirable) in a discipline relevant to survey research and quantitative analysis, such as statistics, biostatistics, econometrics, applied economics, agricultural / environmental / behavioural economics, quantitative research methods, or a related field.

Minimum of 5 years' senior-level experience in the design and technical delivery of primary data collection and quantitative analysis for feasibility, market, or applied research studies in Vietnam, with substantive experience serving as the principal methodological and analytical lead on multi-source, multi-province studies.

Demonstrated experience designing survey instruments, sampling frameworks (including power calculations), enumerator training curricula, and data quality assurance protocols for large-scale primary data collection.

Strong methodological grounding in mixed-methods research design and MEL frameworks, including sampling frameworks, quantitative and qualitative data collection instruments, complex statistical analysis, interpretation, and reporting, and data quality assurance protocols.

Demonstrated experience conducting advanced statistical analyses, including at least one of: probabilistic modelling (Monte Carlo simulation or equivalent), scenario or sensitivity analysis, econometric modelling, or supply reliability modelling.

Substantive technical familiarity with at least one of the following areas relevant to the study: rice systems and rice residue / straw management; low-emission agricultural value chains; biomass, bioenergy, or sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) feedstocks; agri-food supply chain analysis; or climate finance and carbon markets in Vietnamese agriculture.

Working familiarity with recognised international sustainability and carbon accounting frameworks relevant to low-emission agriculture and SAF feedstocks (e.g., ICAO/CORSIA, Gold Standard, or comparable standards) is desirable.

Prior experience in the Mekong Delta is strongly preferred, particularly in An Giang, Đồng Tháp, and Long An provinces.

Strong analytical, writing, and editorial skills, including the ability to translate technical statistical outputs into decision-ready analytical narratives with clearly caveated claims and transparent confidence ranges (sample analytical products may be required).

Advanced proficiency in statistical software such as Stata, R, or Python, and in survey platforms (e.g., ODK, KoBoToolbox, SurveyCTO), as well as MS Office (Word, Excel, PowerPoint).

Excellent command of English (written and spoken) is required to work effectively with the International Team Lead and international co-investment partners.

text:
American Airlines’ recent milestone in collaboration with clean fuels company Infinium puts the spotlight on eSAF, the even-cleaner version of SAF (sustainable aviation fuel). This is eSAF produced locally in Texas, and currently seen as the best option for real reductions in CO2 emissions associated with commercial aviation.

A recent American Airlines flight from Corpus Christi International Airport (CRP) to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) marked an important moment not just for the airline, but for commercial aviation in the US. That’s because it demonstrated the real-world feasibility of something called eSAF, a type of ultra-low carbon electrofuel.

eSAF is not the same as SAF, which is made from different types of bio-based feedstock. eSAF is obtained using waste CO2 and green electricity. Both are drop-in fuels for aircraft, which need to be blended with conventional jet fuel in specific proportions in order to be certified (based on ASTM International’s specification for JetA) for safe use in today’s aircraft engines.

The eSAF for this milestone flight came from Infinium, a clean fuels company operating what is considered the world’s first drop-in eFuels facility. This facility is called Pathfinder, it’s located in Corpus Christi, Texas, and it became operational in 2023. It produces eFuels using renewable electricity from wind and solar resources available in the region, plus waste CO2 provided by Howard Energy Partners, located right next to Project Pathfinder.

This wasn’t just the first real-world deployment of Infinium’s eSAF, but also the first delivery of SAF made without bio-based feedstock to a commercial airport in the US. The eSAF was produced at the Pathfinder facility, blended with commercial jet fuel, then delivered to the existing, standard fueling infrastructure at CRP for the American Airlines passenger flight to DFW.

American Airlines and Infinium have already signed an offtake agreement for commercial volumes of eSAF. This clean jet fuel won’t come from the Pathfinder facility, but from a future facility, Project Roadrunner, located in West Texas. Project Roadrunner will turn an existing gas-to-liquid facility into a clean fuel facility. It will use wind and solar assets purposely-built for its operations, and captured emissions from different operators in the area.

This innovative project is already under construction and set to kick off production and deliveries in 2027, with a planned output of more than 5 million gallons of eSAF annually.

eSAF is only one of Infinium’s clean products, along with eDiesel (for medium and heavy-duty trucks), and eNaphtha (a replacement for petroleum-derived napahtha used in the chemical and industrial sectors, including plastics and solvents production). Infinium’s eSAF for aviation is an ultra-low carbon, energy-dense fuel that can reduce lifecycle GHG emissions by more than 90% compared to fossil-based jet fuel.

title: Why are airlines keeping older aircraft in service for longer? - Aerospace Global News
description:
Why are aircraft delivery delays forcing airlines to keep older fleets?
Older aircraft are less efficient than the latest generation models, but they are still essential during a period of strong travel demand and limited capacity.
For airlines, keeping older aircraft flying has become a necessity rather than a choice.
How long will airlines keep older aircraft in service?
Until aircraft availability improves, airlines will continue relying on older fleets to maintain operations.
text:
What started as a post-pandemic production slowdown has turned into a much bigger challenge for the aviation industry.

Airbus and Boeing are still facing delivery delays, while manufacturers and suppliers continue to deal with shortages of parts, skilled workers and the production capacity needed to build aircraft at the pace airlines need.

Here we dive deeper into why airlines are always looking to (safely) extend aircraft life wherever possible.

Why are aircraft delivery delays forcing airlines to keep older fleets?

Aircraft deliveries remain below the levels required to meet airline demand, leaving thousands of aircraft on order but unavailable for operators.

For airlines, waiting for new aircraft is no longer measured in months; in many cases, it is taking years.

As a result, carriers are changing their fleet strategies. Rather than retiring older aircraft when replacements arrive, many are investing in additional maintenance, cabin upgrades and refurbishment programmes to keep existing fleets flying safely.

New aircraft remain the preferred option because they offer better fuel efficiency, lower maintenance costs and improved passenger experience. However, delayed deliveries have left airlines with limited alternatives.

How are supply chain problems affecting aircraft production?

The shortage of new aircraft also reflects wider disruption across the aviation supply chain. Earlier this year, we reported on A350 delays due to Spirit AeroSystems supply issues as just one example.

Aircraft production depends on thousands of suppliers providing components including engines, avionics and advanced materials. Shortages of parts, workforce challenges and manufacturing bottlenecks have slowed production across the industry.

Engine availability has also become a significant issue, with some airlines facing longer maintenance turnaround times and reduced aircraft availability.

How are airlines keeping aging aircraft in service?

Older aircraft are less efficient than the latest generation models, but they are still essential during a period of strong travel demand and limited capacity.

Airlines are extending aircraft lifespans through heavy maintenance checks, structural inspections, cabin modernisation and technology upgrades. Aircraft that were once expected to leave fleets are now remaining in service for several additional years.

However, ageing fleets come with higher maintenance costs, more reliance on spare parts and increased fuel consumption compared with newer aircraft.

For airlines, keeping older aircraft flying has become a necessity rather than a choice.

What impact is this having on airline operations and growth?

Aircraft shortages are affecting airline plans worldwide. Some carriers have delayed new routes, reduced flight frequencies or postponed expansion because additional aircraft have not arrived as expected.

The limited availability of aircraft has also increased leasing costs, as airlines compete for capacity from a smaller pool of available planes.

For passengers, this can mean fewer schedule options. For airlines, it means managing rising demand with fewer resources.

How do older aircraft affect aviation’s net zero targets?

The biggest concern surrounding delayed aircraft deliveries is their impact on aviation’s climate ambitions.

New generation aircraft are much more fuel-efficient. By keeping ageing fleets in service longer, airlines are delaying some of the emissions reductions expected from fleet renewal.

Fleet replacement remains one of aviation’s most important tools for reducing carbon emissions. Alongside sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), operational improvements and future technologies, newer aircraft are expected to play a key role in achieving net zero emissions by 2050.

How long will airlines keep older aircraft in service?

The aviation industry is already working to increase SAF production, improve efficiency and develop future technologies. However, without enough new aircraft entering service, reducing emissions becomes more difficult.

Airlines are not abandoning their sustainability goals; they are managing a situation where one of the most effective short-term solutions – that is, replacing older aircraft – is being delayed.

Manufacturers are working to increase production, but supply chain pressures are expected to continue for the foreseeable future. Until aircraft availability improves, airlines will continue relying on older fleets to maintain operations.

Extending aircraft lifespans is helping the industry manage today’s challenges, but it’s something of a sticking plaster solution to a much larger problem.
